interactive.title: Scales
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens on grids whose axes carry names, units and numbers that go up in steps other than 1. A point you can drag shows its reading in a label, and on some screens each large square is split into 5 small ones. One screen lets you set what a square up is worth, 1, 2, 5 or 10 L, and watch the same readings fit, squash low or run off the top. Others show uneven labels bending a steady line, and an axis that starts at 228 V. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it.
interactive.ignores: The readings (fuel used, volumes and voltages) are example values, chosen to sit on whole or small squares, not measured from a real engine, tank or supply. Where small squares are drawn, each large square here is split into 5, so count the small squares on any graph you read. Reading values off a curve comes in a later lesson, and logarithmic scales in a later course.

numbers.label: Along, 2 h a square from 0 to 12 h; up, 50 L a square from 0 to 250 L. 4 squares along and 3 up is 4 × 2 = 8 h and 3 × 50 = 150 L, the point (8, 150), in step 1
3 squares along at 2 h and 2 up at 20 L reads 6 h, 40 L, not 3 h, 2 L (squares as 1) or 8 h, 60 L (gridlines counted), in step 2
5 L at 4 h, at 2 h and 5 L a square, is 2 squares along and 1 up, not 4 and 5 (squares as 1) or 4 and 1 (8 h), in step 3
20 L a large square split into 5 small ones: 20 ÷ 5 = 4 L each, so 3 small squares past 40 L is 40 + 3 × 4 = 52 L, in step 4
50 L a large square split into 5: 50 ÷ 5 = 10 L each, so 2 small squares past 150 L is 170 L, not 152 L (small squares as 1) or 160 L (split into 10), in step 5
Readings of 4 L an hour up to 24 L on 5 squares: 1 or 2 L a square runs off the top, 5 L fits, 10 L squashes them low, in step 6
Readings up to 160 L on 5 squares: 160 ÷ 5 = 32, so 50 L a square, not 20 L (to 100 L) or 40 L (small squares of 8 L), in step 7
An example steady fill of 15 L a minute for 6 min, up to 90 L: straight on labels 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100; bent on labels 0, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100, in step 8
10 L an hour read at 0, 1, 2, 3, 5 and 10 h: on labels 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10 it seems to speed up; at 2 h a square it is straight, in step 9
Readings of 229 to 233 V: from 228 V at 1 V a square the 4 V rise spans 4 squares; from 0 at 50 V a square, 0.08 of one, in step 10
A = 229 V and B = 232 V from 228 V: B sits 4 squares up to 1, but is 232 − 229 = 3 V more, not 4 times or 4 V more, in step 11
A point 3 squares along at 2 h and 4 up at 5 L, logged as 3 h, 4 L, reads 3 × 2 = 6 h and 4 × 5 = 20 L, in step 12

explain.text:
On a graph a square need not be worth 1. The numbers along an axis set its [[scale]], what each square is worth, and they go up in equal steps placed in line with the gridlines.[^1] So read them before you count. With 2 h a square along and 50 L a square up, a point 4 squares along and 3 up is 4 × 2 = 8 h and 3 × 50 = 150 L, the point (8, 150). Between two numbers, work out what one small square is worth first. If 40 and 60 are one large square apart and it is split into 5 small squares, each is 20 ÷ 5 = 4, so 3 small squares past 40 reads 52.

To draw a graph you choose the scale. Too small and the readings run off the top, too big and they are squashed into a corner. A guide for science teachers gives a simple rule, each large square worth 1, 2 or 5 times a power of ten,[^2] so 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50 and so on, the smallest that fits. Readings up to 160 L on 5 squares need at least 160 ÷ 5 = 32 L a square, so 50 L. 40 L would fit too, but split into 5 its small squares are 8 L, awkward to read between. An Illinois State University physics handbook lists not sticking with a consistent scale on an axis as a problem to avoid,[^3] and labels that go up 10, 10, 10, then 20 and 50 bend the straight line of a steady fill. Last, check where each axis starts. An axis from 228 V turns a 4 V rise into a steep climb, and the same handbook says that in physics it is often best to show the origin, (0, 0).[^4] Start at 0 when you compare sizes, or want to see whether a line runs through (0, 0).

**Read what a square is worth from the axis numbers before you count, and divide to find a small square. When you draw, take the smallest of 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50 and so on that fits, keep the steps equal, and check where each axis starts.**

practice.text:
**Rule of thumb:** Read the axis numbers first and work out what one square, and one small square, is worth. When you draw an axis from 0, divide the biggest reading by the squares you have, then round up to the next of 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50 and so on.

**Worked example:** Readings run up to 160 L, and the axis has 5 large squares up. 160 ÷ 5 = 32, so a square must be worth at least 32 L. The next of 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50 is 50, so the axis runs 0, 50, 100, 150, 200, 250 L. With 5 small squares to each large one, a small square is 50 ÷ 5 = 10 L, so a point 2 small squares past 150 reads 170 L.

**Common mistakes**
- Taking every square as 1. With 2 h a square along and 5 L up, a point 3 squares along and 4 up is 6 h and 20 L, not 3 h and 4 L. The same goes for small squares. When 50 L splits into 5, each is 10 L, so 2 past 150 is 170 L, not 152 L.
- Picking an awkward scale. 40 L a square fits readings up to 160 L, but split into 5 its small squares are 8 L. The rule is 1, 2 or 5 times a power of ten,[^2] so take 50 L, with small squares of 10 L.
- Uneven steps. Not sticking with a consistent scale is a problem to avoid,[^3] since labels that go up 10, 10, 10, then 20 and 50 bend a steady line.
- Not checking where an axis starts. From 228 V at 1 V a square, readings of 229 V and 232 V sit 1 and 4 squares up, yet the second is only 3 V more.

checks.label: Axes are labelled with numbers, in equal steps, which are placed in line with the gridlines: on every screen, finished, each axis's numbers sit on its gridlines and go up in one equal step, except the broken scale the equal-steps screen shows on purpose

A simple rule is that each large square (main division) should have a value of 1, 2 or 5 multiplied by some power of ten: every even scale in the lesson is one, the scale screen offers 1, 2, 5 and 10 L, and for readings up to 160 L on 5 squares the rule gives 50 L, as 20 L reaches only 100 L and 40 L is not 1, 2 or 5 times a power of ten

Another problem to avoid is not sticking with a consistent scale on an axis: a steady fill lies on a straight line on equal steps but bends on the labels 0, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100, and the tank readings that seem to speed up on time labels 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10 lie straight at 2 h a square, the broken labels in the warning colour

In physics it is often best to show the origin (0,0) in each graph: from 228 V the readings' 4 V rise spans 4 of the 5 squares, bracketed, while drawn from 0 they sit within a tenth of a square of each other; and B, 4 squares up to A's 1 on that axis, is only 3 V more, not 4 times as much

Each puzzle accepts only its own answer, and every wrong answer offered is a named slip: each square or small square taken as 1, the gridlines counted, one axis read as 1 a square, a large square split into 10, a scale too small or not 1, 2 or 5, the bend read as the tank filling faster or a point misread, heights from an axis that starts at 228 V read as the voltages

Every screen, finished, keeps its labels inside the picture and clear of each other and of the points; a right answer's route, sums and label read the point by the axis's steps (4 × 2 = 8 and 3 × 50 = 150 on the first screen, 40 + 3 × 4 = 52 between the marks), and each slip is drawn in the warning colour

Before an answer, nothing in a puzzle's picture gives it away: no route, sum, guide, picked-out number or answer label, no numbers up the side of the choosing puzzle, no broken label marked, and the point to drag starts at the origin

Every demonstration has finished arriving within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion within 2.5 s and a slip within 1 s; parts start at least 0.45 s apart and counted steps at least 0.2 s apart

applied.problem: The 1, 2, 5 list omits the decimals the cited rule allows (0.1, 0.2, 0.5), so readings up to 0.8 A would get 1 A a square; "small squares of 8 L" holds only for a split into 5; uneven labels kink a line, not make a curve.

The rule of thumb divides the biggest reading, true only for an axis from 0 (this lesson shows one from 228 V), and lists no decimals; "small squares are 8 L" needs the split into 5; "1 and 4 squares up" needs the 1 V a square it assumes.
Logarithmic scales are not in a later lesson of this course (i4 to i6 never teach them; the course leaves them for later), so "come in later lessons" is untrue for them.

notes.problem: The second [^3] in explain.text backs "in physics it is often best to show the origin", but source 3 quotes only the consistent-scale line; the same document's own words, "In physics it is often best to show the origin (0,0) in each graph." (research R6), should be added as its quote.

Every reading (fuel, volumes, 229 to 233 V, 15 L a minute, 10 L an hour) is a value chosen for the example, so its kind is "assumed", not "constant"; ignores and the caption already call them example values.
